statement: A coach recorded the weekly practice hours $x$ and the number of free throws made out of $20$, $y$, for $6$ players. $$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline y & 6 & 8 & 9 & 11 & 13 & 4 \end{array}$$ The coach finds the least-squares regression line and the correlation coefficient $r$ for all $6$ players. Then the coach removes the player with $x = 6$ and $y = 4$ and recalculates both using the other $5$ players. Compared with the original results, which of the following describes the new results?

choices.text: The slope decreases, and $r$ moves closer to $1$.
choices.misconception: I saw that the low point was hurting the fit, so r moves closer to 1, but I thought removing a point at the right end would flatten the line, even though that point was dragging the right side of the line down.

choices.text: The slope decreases, and $r$ moves closer to $0$.
choices.misconception: I thought having fewer points always makes the line flatter and the correlation weaker.

choices.text: The slope increases, and $r$ moves closer to $1$.
The slope increases, and $r$ moves closer to $0$.
choices.misconception: I saw that the line gets steeper, but I thought removing any data point always weakens the correlation.

hints: Picture the points. Which one does not follow the pattern of the others?
The first $5$ points rise steadily. The point $(6, 4)$ sits far below that trend at the right end. What does it do to the line and to how well a line fits?
Without $(6, 4)$, the points rise about $1.7$ per hour and lie almost on a line. With it, the line is pulled down at the right and the points scatter.

solutions.reliable: The first five points rise steadily, by about $1.7$ free throws per hour, and lie very close to a line, so for them $r$ is close to $1$ (about $0.99$). The point $(6, 4)$ is far below that trend at the far right, so it pulls the right end of the line down, making the slope much smaller (about $0.2$), and it makes the points fit a line poorly (about $r = 0.11$). Removing it makes the slope increase and moves $r$ closer to $1$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
